g11-mathematics-um1-t1.overview: A relation is any pairing of inputs to outputs — a set of ordered pairs. This topic builds the vocabulary of the whole unit: domain, range, relation vs function, mapping diagrams, and the vertical line test that separates functions from ordinary relations.
objectives: Define relation, domain and range from a set of ordered pairs
Represent relations as graphs, tables, mapping diagrams and equations
Distinguish functions from non-functions
Apply the vertical line test to graphs
Evaluate a function using f(x) notation
g11-mathematics-um1-t1.simple: Take two sets — say students and their IDs. Any rule that pairs some students with some IDs is a relation: a set of ordered pairs (student, ID). The domain is the set of all first components (the inputs); the range is the set of all second components (the outputs). A relation becomes a function when every input has exactly ONE output — no student answers to two different IDs. The classic test on a graph: the vertical line test — if any vertical line hits the curve more than once, one x feeds two y's, so it's not a function. Example: y = x² is a function (each x gives one y); x = y² is NOT (x = 4 accepts y = 2 and y = −2). Function notation: f(x) is 'the output of f on input x' — if f(x) = 2x + 1 then f(3) = 7 (plug in, compute). The domain of a formula is what x-values are allowed: all reals unless something breaks — no division by zero (denominator ≠ 0), no even roots of negatives (x − 3 ≥ 0 for √(x−3)). Relations can be described four ways — ordered pairs, a table, a graph, or an equation — and fluent students move between all four.
g11-mathematics-um1-t1.detailed:
Relations formally. A relation R from set A to set B is a subset of the Cartesian product A × B. Written as ordered pairs: R = {(1,2), (3,4), (5,6)}. Domain(R) = {1,3,5}; Range(R) = {2,4,6}. On a coordinate plane, a relation is any set of points. The arrow diagram (mapping) shows domain elements pointing to range elements — a relation is a function iff every domain element has exactly one arrow leaving it (multiple arrows INTO an element are fine — that's many-to-one, still a function; one-to-many is not).

Functions. A function f: A → B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B. Vocabulary: A is the domain, B the codomain, and the actual outputs form the range (image). f(x) = x² with domain ℝ: codomain ℝ, range [0, ∞). The vertical line test is the geometric version of 'exactly one output': a line x = c meeting the graph twice means two outputs for c. Notation subtleties: f(a) is the value at a, not f times a; the 'input' can be any expression — f(x+1) means substitute x+1 everywhere.

Domain & range of formulas. Natural domain rules: polynomial → ℝ; rational → exclude zeros of the denominator (f(x) = 1/(x−2): x ≠ 2); radical (even index) → radicand ≥ 0 (√(x+3): x ≥ −3); combinations → intersect the restrictions. Range techniques: solve for x in terms of y and see which y allow valid x; complete the square (x² − 4x + 1 = (x−2)² − 3 → range [−3, ∞)); for rational functions, horizontal asymptotes often mark excluded values (f(x) = 1/x never equals 0).

Evaluation & difference quotients. Given f(x) = 3x − 5: f(2) = 1, f(−1) = −8, f(a+h) = 3a + 3h − 5, and the difference quotient [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h = 3 (constant — the slope; this is the seed of calculus). Piecewise functions: different formulas on different intervals — f(x) = { x² if x ≥ 0; −x if x < 0 } — evaluate by checking which piece the input falls in; graph each piece with its endpoint included/excluded (closed vs open dot).

keyTerms.def: any set of ordered pairs (subset of A × B)
relation with exactly one output per input
graph is a function iff no vertical line hits twice

Natural domains exclude zero denominators and negative even radicands; ranges come from completing the square or solving for x. f(x) notation means 'evaluate at x', including piecewise and difference-quotient work.

g11-mathematics-um1-t2.overview: The inverse of a relation swaps every ordered pair: (a,b) → (b,a). Graphically the inverse is the reflection across the line y = x. A function's inverse is a function only when the original is one-to-one — tested by the horizontal line test — and finding the algebraic inverse means solving y = f(x) for x.
objectives: Find the inverse of a relation from pairs, graphs and equations
Explain the y = x reflection property
Use the horizontal line test for one-to-one functions
Compute f⁻¹(x) algebraically and verify f(f⁻¹(x)) = x
State domain/range swapping between f and f⁻¹
g11-mathematics-um1-t2.simple: The inverse relation f⁻¹ flips inputs and outputs: if f sends 3 → 7, then f⁻¹ sends 7 → 3. From ordered pairs, just swap coordinates: f = {(1,4),(2,6)} → f⁻¹ = {(4,1),(6,2)}. On a graph, the inverse is the mirror image across the diagonal line y = x (fold the paper along that line — the two graphs coincide). Algebra: replace f(x) with y, swap x and y, solve for the new y. Example: f(x) = 2x + 3 → y = 2x + 3 → x = 2y + 3 → y = (x − 3)/2 → f⁻¹(x) = (x−3)/2. Check: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2·(x−3)/2 + 3 = x ✓. The catch: the inverse of a function is a function only if no two inputs shared an output — f must be one-to-one (injective). Test on a graph: the horizontal line test — if a horizontal line hits twice, the inverse would have one input with two outputs. That's why f(x) = x² (over all ℝ) has no function inverse — both 3 and −3 give 9 — but restricting the domain to x ≥ 0 gives the inverse √x. Domain and range swap: domain of f = range of f⁻¹ and vice versa.
g11-mathematics-um1-t2.detailed:
Definition and geometry. f⁻¹ = {(y,x) : (x,y) ∈ f}. The point (a,b) on f's graph corresponds to (b,a) on f⁻¹'s — reflection in y = x (the perpendicular-bisector property: swapping coordinates reflects across that line). Consequence: f and f⁻¹ intersect only on y = x (when they intersect at all), and the graphs have swapped slopes: where f has slope m, f⁻¹ has slope 1/m at the reflected point.

One-to-one and existence. f is one-to-one (injective) if f(a) = f(b) forces a = b. Horizontal line test: no horizontal line meets the graph more than once. Strictly monotone functions are one-to-one. If f is one-to-one with domain D and range R, then f⁻¹: R → D exists with f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for all x in D and f(f⁻¹(y)) = y for all y in R — the two cancellation identities define inverses of each other.

Algebraic recipe. (1) y = f(x); (2) interchange x and y; (3) solve for y; (4) rename f⁻¹(x); (5) note the domain of f⁻¹ = range of f. Example with restriction: f(x) = x² + 1, x ≥ 0 → x = y² + 1 → y = √(x − 1) → f⁻¹(x) = √(x−1), domain x ≥ 1. Rational example: f(x) = (2x+1)/(x−3) → x = (2y+1)/(y−3) → xy − 3x = 2y + 1 → y(x−2) = 3x+1 → f⁻¹(x) = (3x+1)/(x−2) — a self-similar form; the asymptotes swap (vertical x=3 ↔ horizontal y=2).

Restricting domains. When f is not one-to-one, mathematicians restrict to a maximal monotone piece: sin on [−π/2, π/2] → arcsin; this is exactly how inverse trig functions are born (Unit 6 territory). The inverse of a non-function relation can still be a relation — e.g. the circle's inverse is itself (symmetric about y = x).

g11-mathematics-um1-t2.summary: The inverse relation swaps every pair's coordinates — geometrically a reflection in y = x. A function has an inverse function exactly when it is one-to-one (horizontal line test); otherwise restrict the domain (as with x² → √x). Algebraically: swap x and y, solve, rename. Domain and range trade places, and the cancellation identities f(f⁻¹(x)) = x verify the work.

g11-mathematics-um1-t3.overview: A tour of the function zoo: polynomial (linear, quadratic), rational, radical, absolute-value, exponential, logarithmic and piecewise functions — their formulas, graphs, domains, ranges and the transformations (shifts, stretches, reflections) that generate every graph from a parent.
objectives: Recognize each function type from its formula and graph
State domains and ranges of the standard families
Apply transformations: f(x)+k, f(x−h), a·f(x), f(−x), −f(x)
Match graphs to formulas using key features
Classify functions as even, odd or neither
g11-mathematics-um1-t3.simple: Every function you'll meet is a relative of a few 'parent' graphs. Linear f(x) = mx + b: a straight line. Quadratic f(x) = ax² + bx + c: a parabola (vertex, axis of symmetry). Polynomial: any power sum — smooth, all-real domain; end behavior comes from the leading term. Rational f(x) = P/Q: fractions with x — vertical asymptotes where Q = 0, horizontal/slant asymptotes at infinity. Radical √x: half a sideways parabola, domain x ≥ 0. Absolute value |x|: a V-shape. Exponential bˣ: rapid growth/decay, horizontal asymptote y = 0, domain ℝ, range (0,∞). Logarithmic log_b x: the exponential's inverse — domain x > 0. Piecewise: different rules on different intervals (the taxi-meter function). The master key is transformation: f(x) + k lifts the graph k up; f(x + k) shifts LEFT k (inside the argument, opposite of what you expect); −f(x) flips over the x-axis; f(−x) flips over the y-axis; a·f(x) stretches vertically (a > 1) or flattens (0 < a < 1). Even functions satisfy f(−x) = f(x) — symmetric about the y-axis (x², |x|); odd satisfy f(−x) = −f(x) — symmetric about the origin (x³, 1/x). Learn ~8 parents + 5 moves and you can sketch hundreds of graphs.
g11-mathematics-um1-t3.detailed:
The families. Polynomial degree n: continuous, smooth, at most n−1 turning points, n real zeros counting multiplicity; even degree → same end behavior both sides (a>0: up/up), odd → opposite (up/down). Linear/quadratic are the degree-1/2 cases. Rational: domain excludes Q's zeros; asymptotes — vertical at unrepeated zeros of Q, horizontal by degree comparison (deg P < deg Q → y = 0; equal → ratio of leading coefficients; one more → slant, found by long division). Radical: √[n]{x} — even n needs x ≥ 0; odd n defined everywhere. Exponential aˣ (a>0, a≠1): passes through (0,1), always positive, increasing if a>1, decreasing if 0

Transformations systematically. y = a·f(b(x − h)) + k: k vertical shift, h horizontal shift (right for minus), a vertical stretch/reflection (a<0 flips over x-axis), b horizontal compression (b>1 squeezes) and f(bx) with b<0 flips over y-axis. Order matters: stretches before shifts. Worked: y = −2f(x+3) + 1 = flip, stretch ×2, left 3, up 1. The 'inside vs outside' rule: changes OUTSIDE the function move the graph vertically as written; changes INSIDE move it horizontally in the opposite direction (because you must compensate the input).

Parity. Even: f(−x) = f(x) — y-axis symmetry (x², cos x, |x|, constants). Odd: f(−x) = −f(x) — origin symmetry (x³, sin x, 1/x, x). Neither: x² + x. Tests: algebraic substitution; graphs: fold on the axis / rotate 180° about origin. Odd functions defined at 0 must have f(0) = 0. Sum/product rules: even+even = even, odd+odd = odd, even×odd = odd (like signs).

keyTerms.def: the simplest member of a family
a line the graph approaches but doesn't reach

g11-mathematics-um1-t3.summary: The function zoo: polynomials (smooth, all reals), rational (asymptotes at denominator zeros), radical (domain from the radicand), absolute value (V), exponential (always positive, y = 0 asymptote), logarithmic (x > 0, inverse of exponential), piecewise (interval rules). Every graph is a parent moved by y = a·f(b(x−h)) + k: outside shifts vertical, inside shifts opposite-horizontal, a stretches/flips vertically, b horizontally. Parity (even/odd) reads symmetry from f(−x).

g11-mathematics-um1-t4.overview: Composition chains functions: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) — apply f first, then g. This topic covers computing compositions from formulas, graphs and tables, finding their domains, decomposing complicated functions into inner/outer parts, and how composition relates to one-to-one and inverse functions.
objectives: Compute (g∘f)(x) from formulas, tables and graphs
Evaluate compositions at specific values
Find the domain of a composite function
Decompose a function into inner and outer components
Explain why composition is not commutative
g11-mathematics-um1-t4.simple: Composition means running one function's output into another's input: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) — f acts first (it's closest to x), then g. If f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = 3x, then g∘f = 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6 (add 2, then triple), while f∘g = 3x + 2 (triple, then add 2) — different! Composition is NOT commutative: order matters, like putting on socks then shoes. From tables: look up f(x), then use that result as an input into g's table. From graphs: read f(x) off the first graph, then find that value on g's x-axis and read its height. Domain: x must be in f's domain AND f(x) must be in g's domain — e.g. with f(x) = √x and g(x) = 1/(x−2): g∘f = 1/(√x − 2) needs x ≥ 0 and √x ≠ 2 → x ≠ 4. Decomposition is the reverse skill: see h(x) = (5x − 1)³ and name f(x) = 5x − 1 (inner), g(x) = x³ (outer) so h = g∘f — the chain-rule anatomy for Grade 12. One elegant fact: a function composed with its inverse gives the identity — f⁻¹∘f = x (the 'undo' property from the previous topic).
g11-mathematics-um1-t4.detailed:
Mechanics. (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)): substitute the whole formula of f wherever g has its variable, then simplify. Worked: f(x) = x² − 1, g(x) = 2x + 3 → g(f(x)) = 2(x² − 1) + 3 = 2x² + 1; f(g(x)) = (2x+3)² − 1 = 4x² + 12x + 8. Evaluation without expanding: (g∘f)(2) = g(f(2)) = g(3) = 9 — the two-step machine. Associativity: (f∘g)∘h = f∘(g∘h) — composition IS associative, so chains are unambiguous. Identity: f∘id = id∘f = f.

Domains. dom(g∘f) = {x ∈ dom f : f(x) ∈ dom g}. Example: f(x) = 1/x, g(x) = √x → g∘f = √(1/x): need x ≠ 0 and 1/x ≥ 0 → x > 0. The domain can be smaller than either piece's natural domain — always intersect the conditions. A common trap: simplifying first can hide restrictions (√(x²) = |x| but the composite's domain may still exclude values).

Decomposition & the chain. Any nested expression is a composition tower: h(x) = sin³(2x + 1) = g∘f∘k with k = 2x+1, f = sin u, g = u³ — decomposition is the prerequisite for the Grade 12 chain rule. Strategy: work from the outside in (last operation applied = outermost function).

Composition and inverses. If f, g are one-to-one, g∘f is one-to-one and (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹ — the inverse of a chain undoes it in reverse order (put socks/shoes on then take them off backwards). Verification of inverses via composition: f and g are inverses iff f∘g = id AND g∘f = id — the cleanest inverse check (stronger than solving for x).

keyTerms.def: the first-applied function in a composite

Discounts: price → 20% off → 10% loyalty off — two functions composed (and order changes the total!)
Physics: time → position → temperature along a path — chained measurements
Computing: function pipelines and map/filter chains are compositions

g11-mathematics-um1-t4.summary: Composition feeds one function into another: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)), f first. It's associative but not commutative. Domains require both the inner function defined AND its output legal for the outer. Decompose nested expressions outside-in (the chain-rule skill). Inverses undo compositions in reverse order, and f∘f = identity marks a self-inverse function.

g11-mathematics-um1-t5.overview: Inverse functions in full: when a function has one, how to compute it algebraically, how to verify by composition, how its graph mirrors the original, and applications — undoing formulas (temperature conversion, decoding, solving for time in growth models).
objectives: Determine whether a function is invertible (one-to-one)
Compute f⁻¹ algebraically with domain restrictions
Verify inverses using both composition identities
Graph f and f⁻¹ using the y = x reflection
Apply inverse functions to undo real formulas
g11-mathematics-um1-t5.simple: An inverse function undoes what f did: if f converts C to F, f⁻¹ converts F back to C. Only one-to-one functions have inverses — every output must come from exactly one input (horizontal line test). The recipe: (1) write y = f(x); (2) swap x and y; (3) solve for y; (4) rename as f⁻¹(x); (5) state its domain (= f's range). Example: f(x) = (x+1)/(x−2) → x = (y+1)/(y−2) → xy − 2x = y + 1 → y(x−1) = 2x+1 → f⁻¹(x) = (2x+1)/(x−1). Verify BOTH ways: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x and f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. Graphically: reflect across y = x — swap every point's coordinates; asymptotes swap too (f's vertical ↔ f⁻¹'s horizontal). Domain restrictions matter: f(x) = x² on x ≥ 0 inverts to √x; on x ≤ 0 it inverts to −√x — the restriction chooses the branch. Real uses: solving for time in N = N₀·2ᵗ needs the log (the inverse of exponential); converting between formulas and their inverses is 'unit conversion' for functions.
g11-mathematics-um1-t5.detailed:
Invertibility. f: A → B invertible ⇔ f is bijective (one-to-one AND onto its range — onto is automatic if we take B = range). One-to-one: f(a)=f(b) → a=b. Continuous functions on an interval are invertible iff strictly monotone. When f isn't one-to-one globally (x², sin x), restrict the domain to a monotone piece — the standard restrictions define √, arcsin, etc.

Computation & verification. The swap-and-solve recipe works when f is one-to-one; if solving gives ±, the sign is chosen by f's domain restriction. Verification: compose both directions — f(f⁻¹(x)) = x for x in dom f⁻¹ AND f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for x in dom f; one direction alone can fail to catch domain errors (classic: f(x)=x², 'inverse' √x — f(√x)=x ✓ but √(x²)=|x| ≠ x ✗ without the restriction).

Graph & calculus previews. Reflection in y = x: (a,b) ↔ (b,a); tangent slopes reciprocate: (f⁻¹)′(b) = 1/f′(a) (Grade 12). Intercepts swap: f's x-intercept is f⁻¹'s y-intercept. If f and f⁻¹ meet, they meet on y = x (for increasing f; decreasing f can meet off the line — a subtlety worth knowing).

Applications. Unit conversions: F = (9/5)C + 32 ↔ C = (5/9)(F − 32). Physics: t = √(2h/g) inverts h = ½gt². Finance: solving for time in compound growth uses the logarithm — the inverse of exponentials (Unit 8's theme). Decoding: cipher E(x) = (ax + b) mod 26 has D = E⁻¹ when gcd(a,26)=1 — invertibility as secrecy.

keyTerms.def: a restricted piece chosen for the inverse
f⁻¹'s graph = f's graph mirrored in y = x

workedExamples.problem: Show f(x) = 4x − 7 is invertible and find f⁻¹.
f(x) = x² − 6x + 5, x ≥ 3. Find f⁻¹.
workedExamples.substitution: f = (x−3)² − 4; y = (x−3)² − 4 → x = 3 + √(y+4) (positive root because x ≥ 3)
workedExamples.answer: f⁻¹(x) = 3 + √(x + 4) with domain x ≥ −4 (= f's range)

workedExamples.problem: Why does f(x) = x² + 1 (no restriction) fail the inverse test?
workedExamples.substitution: f(2) = f(−2) = 5 — the line y = 5 hits twice; swap-solve gives y = ±√(x−1) — two outputs
workedExamples.answer: Not injective; restrict to x ≥ 0 (or ≤ 0) to get √(x−1) (or −√(x−1))

workedExamples.problem: Convert: F = (9/5)C + 32. Find the inverse and use it for 98.6 °F.
workedExamples.answer: Body temperature: 98.6 °F = 37 °C — the inverse formula is the conversion

workedExamples.problem: f⁻¹(x) = √(x − 2). Recover f(x) and its domain.
workedExamples.substitution: y = √(x−2) → x = y² + 2 (y ≥ 0) → f(x) = x² + 2 with domain x ≥ 0

commonMistakes: Inverting non-injective functions without restricting — the ± must be resolved by the domain
Verifying only one composition direction — domain errors hide in the other
Forgetting f⁻¹'s domain = f's range (not f's domain!)
Thinking f⁻¹(x) = 1/f(x) — notation trap again
Reflecting points incorrectly: swap coordinates, don't negate them
Dropping the restriction when writing the final inverse (√(x²) = |x|, not x)
applications: Thermometers and unit conversion: every conversion formula pair is an inverse pair
Cryptography: encryption must be invertible to decrypt — one-to-one is secrecy's requirement
Physics: inverting h(t) to find impact time; inverting lens formulas
Economics: inverting demand P(Q) to get the willingness-to-pay function
Engineering calibration: sensor voltage → temperature via the inverse of the response curve
g11-mathematics-um1-t5.summary: A function is invertible exactly when one-to-one; the inverse undoes it, verified by f∘f⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘f = identity. Compute by swap-and-solve, resolving ± with the domain restriction; the graph is the reflection in y = x, with domains and ranges (and asymptotes) swapped. Non-injective parents (x², sin) get standard restrictions — the birth of √ and arcsin. Real formulas are inverted constantly: unit conversions, decoding, solving for time.

questions.explanation: Fixed points lie on the mirror

questions.q: f(x) = x³ is invertible on ℝ.
Checking f(f⁻¹(x)) = x alone fully verifies inverses.
questions.explanation: The other direction catches domain errors

questions.q: The mirror line for inverse graphs:
Explain why restricting x² to x ≥ 0 is exactly what makes √x a function.
questions.explanation: On [0,∞) every output y ≥ 0 comes from exactly one input, so the swapped relation assigns each x ≥ 0 a single y = √x; without the restriction, x and −x share an output and the swap would give two roots

g11-mathematics-um1-t6.overview: Relations and functions in the real world: modeling with functions, piecewise cost structures, direct and inverse variation, domain/range as practical constraints, and reading function graphs to answer real questions.
objectives: Translate word problems into function notation and formulas
Model piecewise situations (tariffs, taxes, shipping)
Use direct/inverse/joint variation models
Interpret graphs: intervals of increase, maxima, break-even
Judge when a relation model is appropriate
g11-mathematics-um1-t6.simple: Functions are the math of 'depends on'. Strategy for word problems: name the input (independent variable), name the output, find the rule, then clamp the domain to what's physically possible (time ≥ 0, people are whole numbers). Piecewise models are everywhere: a taxi charges a fixed 10 Birr plus 5 Birr/km → C(d) = 10 + 5d; mobile data plans charge a base fee then per-MB rates — different formulas per interval. Variation: direct (y = kx — distance at constant speed), inverse (y = k/x — time vs speed for a fixed trip; price vs quantity for fixed budget), joint (y = kxz), combined (y = kx/z). Reading graphs for decisions: where is profit positive (above the axis)? When is the population growing fastest (steepest climb)? What's the maximum height (peak)? Break-even points are the zeros of profit = revenue − cost. Example: a farmer fences a rectangle against a river with 120 m of fence: area A(L) = L(120 − 2L) — a quadratic whose domain is 0 < L < 60, maximized at L = 30 (A = 1800 m²). The function is the model; the domain, range and graph are the answer's grammar.
g11-mathematics-um1-t6.detailed:
Modeling cycle. Real situation → identify variables → choose a family (linear for constant rates, quadratic for area/projectile/optimum, exponential for growth/decay, rational for sharing/averages, piecewise for tiered rules) → fit the formula (from data points or given rates) → constrain the domain → interpret: predict, optimize, decide → validate against reality. Each step has a failure mode: wrong family (linear when diminishing returns apply), ignored domain (negative time), over-reading the model (extrapolating beyond data).

Piecewise economics. Tiered tariffs: electricity with blocks (first 100 kWh at rate a, next at b) — the bill is a continuous piecewise-linear function with changing slope. Shipping: flat rates per weight band — a step function (discontinuous jumps). Tax brackets: marginal rates — total tax = sum of pieces. The exam favorite: cell-phone plans compared as two lines — the break-even usage is their intersection.

Variation. Direct: y = kx (k constant) — graph through origin; 'proportional'. Inverse: xy = k — hyperbola; joint: y = kxz; combined: y = kx/z² (Newton's gravitation form). Method: write the model with k, plug one known pair to find k, then predict. Example: if 5 workers build a wall in 12 days, time is inversely proportional to workers: T = 60/w → 10 workers = 6 days (with the domain w ≥ 1, integer).

Optimization sketches. Quadratic models peak at the vertex: fenced area, revenue = price × demand (linear demand → quadratic revenue), projectile height. The completing-the-square or vertex formula x = −b/2a gives the optimum; the domain decides whether the vertex is reachable. Graph interpretation questions: increasing/decreasing intervals, local max/min, average rate of change = slope of the secant between two points — the bridge to Grade 12 calculus.

keyTerms.def: y = k/x — one grows as the other shrinks

workedExamples.problem: A bus fare is 25 Birr plus 3 Birr per km. Write C(d), state the domain, find the cost of 40 km.
workedExamples.answer: C(d) = 25 + 3d (d ≥ 0); 40 km costs 145 Birr

workedExamples.problem: Plan A: 300 Birr + 1 Birr/MB. Plan B: 500 Birr + 0.5 Birr/MB. When is B cheaper?
workedExamples.answer: Break-even at 400 MB; heavy users save with B

workedExamples.problem: If y varies inversely as x and y = 8 when x = 3, find y when x = 6.
workedExamples.answer: y = 4 — doubling x halves y

workedExamples.problem: A 200 m fence encloses a rectangle along a straight river (no fence on the river side). Maximize area.
workedExamples.answer: 50 m × 100 m → 5000 m² maximum

workedExamples.problem: Water temperature in a pot: rises linearly to 100 °C in 10 min, then stays at 100. Write the piecewise model and sketch.
workedExamples.substitution: T(t) = 20 + 8t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10 (from 20 °C); T = 100 for t > 10
workedExamples.answer: Ramp then plateau — a continuous piecewise function

commonMistakes: Ignoring domain constraints — negative time, fractional people, impossible prices
Mixing marginal and average in tiered pricing (tax brackets apply per band, not to the total)
In inverse variation, writing y = kx instead of y = k/x — check which grows
Assuming the vertex is the max even outside the domain — clamp first
Reading 'increasing' as 'positive' — a function can increase while negative
Forgetting units — the model's numbers are meaningless without them
applications: Telecom: Ethiopia's mobile data bundles are piecewise cost functions
Agriculture: yield vs spacing models (quadratic with optimum)
Transport: fuel cost vs speed — the inverse-then-direct trade-off
Business: break-even analysis — zeros of revenue minus cost
Health: drug dosage intervals modeled by piecewise decay
g11-mathematics-um1-t6.summary: Real-world functions: name input/output, pick the family (linear rates, quadratic optima, exponential growth, rational sharing, piecewise tiers), clamp the domain to reality. Variation models (direct kx, inverse k/x, joint/combined) find k from one pair. Decisions come from reading graphs — intersections (break-even), vertices (optima), intervals of increase, secant slopes (average rates). The modeling cycle ends by validating against the situation.
